rounds.text: Rachit Prints Ltd trades at a P/E of 10.56x against a sector benchmark of 15.53x and an EV/EBITDA of 6.71x against a sector benchmark of 9.17x, presenting an attractive entry valuation relative to peers [E6, E11]. The business demonstrates exceptional capital efficiency with an ROE of 19.4% and an ROCE of 20.79%, comfortably outperforming their respective sector benchmarks of 6.43% and 7.96% [E9, E10]. Growth metrics remain robust, evidenced by a 3-year compounded sales growth of 18% and a multi-year profit uptrend underpinned by a 143% compounded profit growth over 3 years [E14, E16, E47]. Furthermore, a discounted cash flow model indicates an intrinsic value of Rs 379 per share against a market price of Rs 179, establishing a substantial margin of safety of 52.7% [E34, E35]. Conceded: [E25] and [E27] show negative operating cash flow of Rs -3.60 Cr and negative free cash flow of Rs -12.70 Cr for Mar 2026. Conceded: [E43] indicates working capital days have increased from 72.6 days to 133 days.

Despite reported profits, the company is bleeding cash, posting a severe negative operating cash flow of Rs -3.60 Cr and a free cash flow of Rs -12.70 Cr in Mar 2026 [E27]. This translates to a dismal cash conversion of -0.79x against reported profit, with operating cash flow making up only -15% of operating profit [E25, E28]. Compounded profit growth has ground to a sudden halt, dropping to just 1% over the trailing twelve months [E17]. Operational efficiency is also deteriorating as working capital days have ballooned significantly from 72.6 days to 133 days [E43]. Furthermore, financial quality flags indicate that the company might be capitalizing its interest cost alongside paying a 0.00% dividend yield despite reporting repeated profits [E4, E41, E42]. Expectations are running dangerously ahead of actual business delivery, with recent price growth exceeding profit growth by 80% [E38]. Conceded: the company maintains solid historical return metrics, including a 3-year median ROE of 30% and an 18% compounded sales growth rate over 3 years [E14, E20].

The bear’s focus on short-term cash flow ignores the company’s structural profitability, as evidenced by a robust 19.4% ROE and 20.79% ROCE, both of which significantly outperform sector benchmarks [E9, E10, E13]. While the bear highlights a single year of cash flow pressure, it overlooks the multi-year trend of 143% compounded profit growth and 18% sales growth, demonstrating a proven ability to scale operations [E14, E16]. The concern regarding working capital is countered by the company’s consistent ability to expand operating margins by 10 percentage points over three years, proving that management is successfully capturing value despite temporary fluctuations [E22]. Conceded: the company reported negative operating cash flow of Rs -3.60 Cr and free cash flow of Rs -12.70 Cr in Mar 2026 [E26, E27]. Conceded: the dividend yield is 0.00% and working capital days have increased to 133 days [E4, E43]. These short-term liquidity challenges are mitigated by the fact that the stock trades at a significant discount to its intrinsic value, with a 52.7% margin of safety, suggesting the market has overreacted to recent volatility [E34, E35]. Ultimately, the company’s valuation remains attractive, with an EV/EBITDA of 6.71x compared to the sector benchmark of 9.17x, indicating that the market is failing to price in the firm's superior capital efficiency [E11].

The bull’s reliance on historical ROE and ROCE [E9, E10] ignores the reality that these metrics are currently decoupled from actual cash generation, as evidenced by the negative operating cash flow of Rs -3.60 Cr and free cash flow of Rs -12.70 Cr in Mar 2026 [E26, E27]. While the bull cites multi-year profit growth [E16], it fails to address that this momentum has stalled, with compounded profit growth over the trailing twelve months plummeting to just 1% [E17]. Conceded: the company has achieved a 10 percentage point expansion in operating margins over three years [E22]. However, this margin expansion is undermined by the fact that operating cash flow is now -15% of operating profit, suggesting that reported profits are not being converted into liquid assets [E28]. The bull’s dismissal of working capital concerns is contradicted by the sharp increase in working capital days from 72.6 to 133 days [E43], which, combined with the potential capitalization of interest costs [E42], raises significant questions about the quality of the company's earnings.
